title: Bauza's view of Kenton's music
summary: He says marrying American harmony and Cuban rhythm requires deep knowledge, and Kenton's band could not swing.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Yeah. Can you talk a little about -- what were your views on Kenton and what he was trying to do?

Well, he would (inaudible) because he would (inaudible), he said, Mario, you know, American music has progressed a whole lot harmonically, but rhythm-wise remained the same. So he was getting into this idea, do you want to (inaudible) influence this.

The only thing -- I told him, you know, the only problem is, to really get into the nitty gritty, you've got to know a whole lot about one thing, in order to get the agreed marriage. Otherwise, it's never going to sound right, because the average drummer cannot play with a conga beside them -- too much against Syncopation (inaudible). They turn off; they cannot play.

And they don't sound like this and don't sound like that. And then the American musicians, they got a conception about Cuban music, (inaudible), that's what they think about. (Inaudible). But they were completely wrong. So I went a

couple of times to their rehearsal, and, you know, they all liked me and (inaudible) but with that band (inaudible) good piano, Afro-Cuban. Let's face it, because the jazz band never was good, because the band was too clumsy. There was not a player, as you say, I would call a modern version of Paul Whiteman with more excitement (inaudible). They went for a climax and harmony, you know what I mean, dynamics this different (inaudible). You could call that dance -- but nobody could dance by that band. There was no rhythm in that band. (Inaudible).

So he tried the other rhythm, and the other rhythm (inaudible). Up to today that (inaudible) never, never, never could swing (inaudible) band for kids (inaudible) or the brass AND THAT WAS THAT. (inaudible).
